sections.html:
Bonneville County's seat, Idaho Falls, ranks fourth among Idaho cities by population. It had 64,818 residents in the 2020 census and an estimated 71,785 in 2025, and the surrounding metro area held 154,855 people in 2020. Shopping, culture and health care for Eastern Idaho all flow through town. The Idaho National Laboratory, with more than 8,000 employees across its desert site and a research campus in town, anchors the job market.

The Snake River runs through the city, which sits at about 4,712 feet. Altitude affects what buyers check in a house, from heating to freeze protection.

Here the heating bill and the roof matter more than air conditioning. A typical year at the airport weather station brings 10.07 inches of precipitation, including 36.9 inches of snow. The January low averages 12.1 degrees Fahrenheit, the July high averages 86.6, and the coldest reading on record is minus 51.

Inspectors focus on the furnace, attic insulation, window seals and whatever can freeze: outdoor hose bibs, and supply lines running through crawl spaces. Severe weather is uncommon, though an F2 tornado struck the area on April 7, 1978. Check your own insurance history for hail and wind claims on the roof before you list.

Idaho Falls is usually described by a handful of areas, each with its own housing stock.

  • Downtown: the historic townsite on the east side of the river.
  • The Numbered Streets: the first planned neighborhood, between South Boulevard and Holmes Avenue, including the Eleventh Street Historic District.
  • West Side: the area around the Idaho Falls Regional Airport.
  • Snake River Landing: a large mixed-use development west of the river near I-15, with homes, restaurants, parks and the Mountain America Center.

Expect older Numbered Streets houses to come with postponed upkeep, which a cash buyer prices in. Subdivisions farther out are generally newer and need less. Idaho Falls School District 91 serves the city, with more than 10,000 students in 19 schools. Confirm boundaries with the district if a buyer asks.

sections.h2: Utilities when you sell or move out
sections.html:
Because the city owns the electric utility, starting or stopping service is a City Hall errand at 308 Constitution Way. Idaho Falls Power has served the city since 1900 and owns five hydropower plants supplying about one-third of the city's electricity. Electric, water, sanitation and wastewater come on one bill, and you can close an account by signing in to the customer self-service portal with your existing account.

Recent upgrades add a step. To get power turned back on after finishing electrical work, you need the city's electrical inspectors at the Building Department to inspect it. Once it passes, a connect order goes to Idaho Falls Power. Work done without a permit can hold up a sale or a restart, so find out from the Building Division what is on file before listing.

  • Wait to close or transfer service until the sale date is fixed, and never before the buyer's final walkthrough.
  • Leave power and water running through closing so inspections and appraisals can go ahead.
  • Collect permit records for work on the panel, furnace or water heater.

Bonneville County sends the bill, and none of the money goes to the state. The county levies and collects on behalf of the cities, school districts and other taxing districts. Your house is valued at 100% of market value, less exemptions, as of January 1. Yearly swings in value are not capped by law. What is capped is how fast a district can grow the property tax part of its budget: 3%, unless voters approve more or new construction and annexation widen the base.

DateWhat happens in Bonneville County
January 1Lien date used to set market value
April 15Application deadline for the homeowner's exemption or property tax reduction
First Monday in JuneAssessor mails assessment notices
Fourth Monday in JuneAppeals to the Board of Equalization must be in
December 20Pay everything, or the first half
June 20Pay the second half if you paid the first

Homeowners get 50% off the value of the house and up to one acre, with a $125,000 ceiling. Once title changes hands or you move out, the benefit ends and the buyer files for their own. Have the title company prorate taxes at closing. A value you dispute goes first to the assessor, then to the Board of Equalization, then to the State Board of Tax Appeals or district court within 30 days.

sections.h2: What an Idaho Falls seller must disclose
sections.html:
Idaho's Property Condition Disclosure Act, Idaho Code 55-2504, requires a completed condition form from anyone selling one to four unit residential property. It applies to sales, exchanges, installment contracts and options to buy, and to rentals the owner does not occupy.

Exemptions appear in Idaho Code 55-2505. They include a fiduciary settling an estate, foreclosure, transfer to a spouse or lineal relative, and an heir who has stayed out of the home for the past year. If one fits, you may not need the form, though an Idaho attorney or title officer should confirm.

This is where listed sales and as-is sales diverge. After the form is signed, a buyer's inspector and lender may demand repairs. Buying the house in its present condition for cash removes that negotiation, although the disclosure rules still govern the transfer.

Lay the numbers side by side. For a listing, estimate repairs a buyer's lender would require, months of utilities and taxes while the house sits, and the work of staging and showings. For a cash offer, use the figure on paper and the closing date you can live with.

Idaho Falls sellers also gain from a simple habit: keep a folder with the tax notice, the last electric bill, permit receipts and any inspection reports. It speeds up every conversation with a buyer, an appraiser or a title officer, and it shows a cash buyer that the house has been looked after.

Winter timing deserves a thought. Snow covers roofs and yards from late autumn, so showings in deep cold reveal less of the house, and a buyer who cannot see the ground may ask for a lower price to cover unknowns. If your date is firm, a direct offer avoids that guessing game.

Then ask three practical questions. Do I owe back taxes or a lien that the title company must pay? Is anyone living in the house who needs time to move? Are there permits missing for electrical or other work that would surface at an inspection? Settling these first keeps a closing on schedule whichever route you choose.

No loan approval stands in the way, so title work and your calendar set the pace. You ask for an offer, the buyer looks at the house, and if you say yes a title or escrow company clears title, drafts the paperwork and closes.

  1. Tell the buyer the address, the condition, whether liens or back taxes exist and whether tenants are in the house.
  2. Weigh the offer against what a listing would cost in commissions, repairs and carrying expenses.
  3. Pick a closing date. The title company settles any mortgage or tax balance out of the proceeds.

Turning an offer down costs nothing. Whether cash or a listing comes out ahead depends on the house, so a local agent's second opinion can help.

faqs.q: How many people live in Idaho Falls?
faqs.a: The 2025 estimate is 71,785 residents. The 2020 census counted 64,818, and the wider metro area had 154,855 people.

faqs.q: When are Bonneville County property taxes due?
faqs.a: Pay the full amount by December 20, or pay at least half then and the rest by June 20 of the following year.

faqs.q: Do I have to fill out a disclosure form to sell my Idaho Falls house?
faqs.a: Usually. Idaho Code 55-2504 covers one to four unit residential property, and section 55-2505 exempts cases like estate transfers and some inherited homes.

faqs.q: How do I shut off utilities when I sell in Idaho Falls?
faqs.a: Sign in to the city's customer self-service portal with your existing account to close service. Electric, water, sanitation and wastewater are handled together at City Hall, 308 Constitution Way.

faqs.q: Does the homeowner's exemption transfer to the buyer?
faqs.a: No. It ends when ownership changes or you stop living in the home as your primary residence, so the buyer applies separately with the county assessor.
